## Summary

The voltage divider was outputting 0.83V instead of 3.3V because R2 was incorrectly set to 2k ohms; changing it to 20k ohms provides the correct 3.3V reference output from the 5V supply (via the standard voltage divider formula: Vout = Vin × R2/(R1+R2) = 5 × 20k/30k ≈ 3.33V).

Perfect! The fix is complete. 

**Summary:** The status LED circuit had a 30 Ω current-limiting resistor which allowed 100 mA through the LED; I changed it to 300 Ω to limit the current to the intended 10 mA operating point and keep it safely under the 20 mA maximum rating.

Excellent! The fix is complete. The issue was that the LED's anode and cathode nodes were reversed in the circuit netlist, preventing current from flowing through the LED even though the power rail was at 5V.

**Summary:** The status LED was not conducting because the diode nodes were reversed in the netlist—it should be `D1 a 0 VF=2.0` (anode at node `a`, cathode at ground) instead of `D1 0 a VF=2.0`, allowing the proper forward current of 10 mA to flow.

Excellent! The fix is complete.

## Summary

The bug was that the 1 kHz anti-aliasing low-pass filter had its capacitor value set too low (10n instead of 100n), making the cutoff frequency approximately 10 kHz instead of 1 kHz. I corrected the capacitor value from 10n to 100n to achieve the proper 1 kHz cutoff frequency, which provides adequate attenuation at 5 kHz as intended for an anti-aliasing filter.

## Summary

The bug in the gain-of-11 sensor amplifier has been fixed by correcting the non-inverting amplifier netlist: the ground resistor (RG) was incorrectly connected between the feedback node and the output node instead of between the feedback node and ground, preventing the proper gain formula (1 + RF/RG) from being applied.

## Summary

The bug was in the pull-up resistor netlist: the resistor was incorrectly connected from `pin` to ground (`0`), making it a pull-down resistor instead of a pull-up. I fixed it by changing `RPU pin 0 10k` to `RPU pin vdd 10k`, so the resistor now properly connects the pin to the 3.3V supply, allowing it to read high when the button is released and low when pressed.

Perfect! The bug has been fixed successfully.

## Summary

The high-pass filter circuit had its resistor and capacitor positions reversed - it was configured as a low-pass filter instead of a high-pass filter. I fixed it by swapping the component connections: the capacitor now connects from input to output (C1 in out 159n) and the resistor connects from output to ground (R1 out 0 1k), which is the correct topology for a high-pass filter that passes high frequencies and blocks low frequencies.

Excellent! All tests pass. 

## Summary

The bug was in the inverting amplifier netlist: the input resistor `RIN` was incorrectly connected between the input node and output node (`RIN in out`), which bypassed the op-amp's feedback circuit. The fix was to connect it between the input node and the inverting input of the op-amp (`RIN in inv`), so the feedback network can properly establish the gain relationship.
